column1: Why is the conversion of photons to digital values at the sensor considered 'irreversible'?
column2: Because each photodiode's accumulated electrons are converted once by the ADC into a fixed-bit integer; any scene detail not captured in that exposure (e.g., blown highlights or crushed shadows) cannot be recovered later in post-production.

column1: What is the Bayer pattern and why does it matter for RAW vs. compressed footage?
column2: A checkerboard of red, green, and blue filters over the sensor so each pixel records only one color channel. Demosaicing reconstructs full RGB/YCbCr data via interpolation. RAW files defer this demosaicing to post-production software, giving the editor explicit control, whereas compressed formats bake in the camera's internal demosaicing algorithm.

column1: How many stops of dynamic range does the human eye perceive versus a typical modern cinema camera?
column2: The human eye perceives roughly 10–14 stops simultaneously; modern cinema cameras typically capture about 12–14 stops, a deliberate balance of sensor physics, signal-to-noise behavior, and grading flexibility.

column1: At 24 fps, what real-world motion frequency triggers temporal aliasing (e.g., the 'wagon-wheel effect')?
column2: Motion faster than half the Nyquist frequency, approximately 12 cycles per second, aliases—causing rotating objects like wheels to appear to spin backward or freeze.

column1: What is the Kuleshov Effect and what cognitive mechanism explains it?
column2: The phenomenon where the same shot (e.g., a neutral face) acquires different emotional meaning depending on the shot it's juxtaposed with. It reflects predictive coding: the visual cortex generates context-based expectations, and perceived meaning emerges from resolving prediction errors.

column1: What is the Phi Phenomenon and why does it enable motion pictures to work?
column2: The perceptual illusion of continuous motion created when discrete images are presented at sufficient temporal density (24–60 fps). It arises from the temporal resolution limits of retinal ganglion cells (~50ms) and cortical processing delays, causing the brain to integrate discrete frames into apparent motion.

column1: What is the approximate conscious information processing rate of human attention, and why does this matter for editing?
column2: Roughly 40–50 bits/second, despite the eyes capturing ~10 million bits/second. Editing acts as an attentional guidance system, selecting viewpoint, duration, and transitions to direct the viewer's limited cognitive bandwidth.

column1: What are the three dimensions of temporal discontinuity created by every edit?
column2: Δt (time compression/expansion: ratio of story time to screen time), Δs (spatial displacement: angular/distance change between camera positions), and Δi (information density: rate of new visual/narrative elements introduced).

column1: What are the approximate minimum and maximum effective shot durations, and why?
column2: Minimum ~0.5 seconds (below this, conscious recognition fails); maximum ~8–12 seconds before attention wanders (absent new information or motion), per the shot-duration formula t_optimal ≈ I/R + t_saccade + t_recognition.

column1: In the audio post-production mixing hierarchy, which element always wins when competing for the same frequency space or dynamic range, and why?
column2: Dialogue always wins. The governing invariant is the primacy of intelligibility over aesthetic pleasure—narrative comprehension depends on audience understanding spoken words, so the hierarchy is dialogue first, music second, effects third.

column1: Why does audio-video synchronization require frame-accurate timecode rather than approximate alignment?
column2: Because picture imposes an absolute temporal reference (exact frames for lip movements, door closes, explosions), unlike flexible musical tempo. Audio must lock to these visual events with zero drift across the entire program, requiring a universal frame-addressing system (timecode) and robust sync protocols across facilities.

column1: What are the three physical constraints that govern video output/delivery format decisions, and how do they trade off?
column2: Bandwidth (data rate, Mbps), storage (capacity, GB/TB), and perceptual fidelity (how closely delivered image matches creative intent). They are in perpetual tension: raising bitrate preserves fidelity but increases bandwidth/storage demand; lowering bitrate saves bandwidth/storage but introduces artifacts like banding, mosquito noise, and temporal stuttering.
